bp: A security camera is useful only if later viewers can trust that the saved footage is the same footage the camera recorded. That matters in courts, insurance claims, workplace investigations, public safety reviews, and compliance checks, where a short clip can change what people believe happened. Generative AI makes this harder because fake or altered video can look convincing, and many viewers do not have the training to notice small signs of manipulation. This paper serves the part of that problem that begins after capture. It does not claim to prove every step from the sensor outward. Instead, it asks for a practical record that makes later tampering detectable. The system records proof about video segments on a public ledger, a shared append-only record, and stores footage through IPFS, a decentralized file network. The point is to make evidence depend less on one camera vendor, one storage server, or one administrator's word.
wh: The hard part is that video evidence has two conflicting needs. It must be available when someone needs to inspect it, but it must also be protected from quiet changes after the fact. A normal storage server can hold the footage, but the same central control that makes storage convenient also creates a trust bottleneck. Someone with access might replace a segment, delete it, or claim a later copy is original. Full camera-capture provenance is even stronger because it follows the evidence from sensor to storage, but that is a larger trust boundary: the camera hardware, capture software, network path, and storage system all have to be controlled and checked. This paper narrows the problem. It accepts that capture itself is outside its guarantee and focuses on post-capture tampering. That narrower promise is still difficult because the log must be hard to rewrite, storage must not depend on one machine, and the delays and transaction fees must remain usable.
naive: A smart beginner might save each camera clip to a cloud drive and keep a spreadsheet saying when each file arrived. That gives a record, but it asks everyone to trust the drive owner and the spreadsheet editor. Another beginner move is to run an AI fake detector on suspicious videos. That can help, but it turns the problem into a guessing contest against future editing tools. The paper's abstract argues for a different baseline: make tampering visible by registering evidence before the dispute. The naive storage-only answer fails because a copied or replaced file may still look normal, and the naive detection-only answer fails because convincing fake media can keep improving.
ap: The core idea is to turn each piece of security footage into a checked package with two separated duties. The footage itself is stored in IPFS, which is a network where files are addressed by their content rather than by the name of one server. A compact fingerprint of the footage and its registration event is written to Binance Smart Chain, a blockchain whose shared record is difficult to rewrite after many participants have accepted it. Later, a verifier does not need to trust a story about the file. The verifier can recompute the file's fingerprint and compare it with the public log. If the footage changed after registration, the comparison should fail. This is why the paper calls the system tamper evident rather than tamper impossible: it cannot stop every attacker from editing a copy, but it is meant to make the edited copy unable to pass as the registered original.
mech: The mechanism starts when a security camera stream is divided into footage segments. Each segment is treated as a piece of evidence that needs a stable identity. The system computes a cryptographic hash, a short fingerprint produced from the file's bits. The important property is that a tiny change in the video should produce a very different fingerprint, so the fingerprint can stand in for the whole file during checking. The segment is uploaded to IPFS, where the file can be retrieved through a content-based address rather than from only one owner's server. The system then registers evidence on Binance Smart Chain. The abstract says this uses cryptographic logging, so the chain stores a verifiable record tied to the footage rather than storing all video bytes directly. When someone later wants to check a clip, the system retrieves or receives the claimed footage, recomputes its hash, and compares that new fingerprint with the logged value. A match supports the claim that this is the same post-capture segment that was registered. A mismatch signals tampering, corruption, or substitution. The prototype evaluation then stresses this pipeline by measuring two practical outputs: cost per registration and delay. The reported bottleneck is IPFS upload time, averaging 2.08 seconds per segment, while the baseline chain transaction fee is about 0.57 USD.
math: The main mathematical idea is one-way fingerprinting. A hash function is a rule that turns a large file into a short string. It is easy to compute the string from the file, but the system relies on it being infeasible to start from the string and build a different convincing file with the same string. It also relies on change sensitivity: if one bit of a video segment changes, the resulting string should look unrelated. That lets a small record protect a large object. The second idea is an append-only public ledger. A blockchain is a shared sequence of records where later records are tied to earlier ones, making quiet rewriting costly because many participants would have to accept the changed history. The third idea is content addressing in IPFS: the address points to what the file is, through its content fingerprint, not merely where a server says it is. The tradeoff is integrity versus cost and delay. Strong public logging buys independent verification, but every registered segment can cost money, and decentralized storage adds waiting time. The math fits because the real question is equality over time: is this file exactly the one that was registered?
dots: This paper sits in the conference's misinformation and trust thread because it treats fake media as a broken evidence chain, not only as a visual classification problem. It is close to provenance work for AI-generated content in the repo: both attach records to content so later systems can ask where something came from instead of only guessing whether it looks false. It also connects to blockchain security papers, but its use of a chain is different from fraud detection or consensus attacks. Here the chain is an audit surface, a place to make a timestamped integrity claim difficult to erase. The IPFS connection links it to decentralized web papers where storage is resilient but introduces new operational problems, including gateway dependence, persistence, and delay. Mathematically, it belongs beside papers about privacy, security, and systems tradeoffs: useful evidence must cross a boundary, private or bulky data should not all live on-chain, and the scarce resources are time, money, storage, and institutional trust.
ww: It works over the naive approach because it separates trust in the video from trust in the storage operator. If a file is merely saved in a database, the database owner can become the judge of its own honesty. With public logging, the verifier has an outside reference point: the recorded fingerprint and time of registration. The reason this helps is simple. An edited video is still a video, and it may still look plausible to people or detection software, but it should not have the same fingerprint as the registered segment. IPFS adds a second benefit by reducing dependence on one storage location. The file can be fetched by content identity, while the chain carries the integrity record. The paper's careful boundary makes the claim more believable. It does not promise to solve sensor compromise, fake footage created before registration, or end-to-end camera provenance. It promises detectable post-capture changes, and the hash-plus-ledger design is well matched to exactly that promise.
po: The payoff is a working evidence pipeline for security and compliance settings where footage may later be challenged. The system gives investigators, auditors, or organizations a way to check whether a registered segment has changed after capture without relying only on the camera operator's storage system. The prototype and stress tests ground the claim in operating measurements, not just architecture. The abstract reports integrity guarantees, an IPFS upload delay averaging 2.08 seconds per segment, and a baseline transaction fee around 0.57 USD. That makes the design most plausible for high-value evidence, where verification is worth paying for.
limits: The main limit is the trust boundary. The system catches post-capture tampering, but it does not prove that the camera saw the real world honestly, that the camera clock was correct, or that fake footage was not registered as if it were genuine. It also depends on hash functions, blockchain records, and IPFS storage behaving as intended. The abstract identifies IPFS upload delay as the main speed bottleneck, so frequent high-resolution segments may strain real-time use. Cost is another assumption: about 0.57 USD per transaction may be viable for important evidence but not for every camera segment at large scale, and the truncated abstract only indicates that Layer 2 help is needed without proving it.
